doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Moving to Orlando and Disney World
summary: He moves to Florida with his family after work dries up in New Jersey and gets a full-time Disney musician job.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: You spent quite a few years at Disney World?
And I think I read in some of your bio information that they eventually cut back on their music?

I went to Florida in 1985. I’d gotten married and had a kid. P.J. was born in October of ’84. Sorry October of ’85. And we were living in Flemington, New Jersey at the time. And I was working in Allentown with a guy named Parke Frankenfield who was big in the Lehigh Valley area. Again, a band organizer who had a big band, a small group, and a steady Friday and Saturday with this quartet. And he played keyboards at the time, although he was mostly a trombone player. A jack of all trades. He played everything. And I was also working in the summer at Great Adventure amusement park in Jackson, New Jersey. So Flemington was half way between the two. So newly married, with a new kid, Great Adventure was closing for the season and Parke Frankenfield was moving to Vero Beach, Florida. And all my work was gone. I was doing Monday nights with Woody Allen at the old Michael’s Pub on 53rd street for $50 on Monday nights. And that was the extent of my gigs. I had a wife and a kid. So I had gone to the Sacramento festival with Parke Frankenfield, the Sacramento Jubilee, which at the time was the largest jazz festival, about 120 bands and 50 stages. It was my first jazz festival I’ve gone to. I was like this is amazing. And I met some guys from Orlando who were there with the Rosie O’Grady’s band. Bill Allred being one of them, the trombone player. And especially Davey Jones became a quick friend of mine. I met them. He said, “where are you from and why don’t you move to Orlando?” And I went well okay. He goes, “come down, stay at my house, I’ll take you all over and introduce you to everybody.” It was a huge music scene. Not a jazz scene, just making your living in the trenches in the music business. Conventions, and theme parks were there. Universal wasn’t there but Disney was there. And at the time Disney had 400 full time musicians. Salary and benefits. No hourly wage and benefits. And I went down and tried out for Disney and stayed at Davey’s house and tried out for Disney. And they were like, “okay move down here and we’ll status you.” You know, because it is a corporation, a large corporation. You’ve got to go through all the initiation, not initiation but orientation and get your I.D. cards and get on the books and all that stuff. I went down there and moved down there with my wife of a year and a half and my son who was three months old, in December of 1985. And in April of 1986 I had a full time job at Disney. In four months. In the meantime I

had worked around town and played at Rosie O’Grady’s and started doing conventions, got to know the contractors in town. Disney had 400 full time musicians there at the time, and now, 30 years later, they’re down to 65 I think, full time musicians. They’ve just cut a lot of the entertainment. As I understand it, just as I moved to town, Operations, Disney World Operations had taken over entertainment, and they knew nothing about entertainment. They are wondering why are all these people sitting around in between shows? They just did a 20 minute show, soaking wet from the heat and the humidity. It feels like 130° outside, and they’re wondering why we aren’t doing something in between shows.
